178931572.title: File:Night-time road resurfacing operation during Chatham Waterfront Bus Station improvement works showing Tarmac vehicles, workers, and road closure on Globe Lane, Chatham, Kent, England.jpg

ObjectName.value: Night-time road resurfacing operation during Chatham Waterfront Bus Station improvement works showing Tarmac vehicles, workers, and road closure on Globe Lane, Chatham, Kent, England

Categories.value: Closed-circuit television (CCTV)|Images with annotations|Chatham Waterfront bus station|Self-published work|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation (51° N, 0° E)|Taken with iPhone 14 Pro|Road closed signs|Night in Chatham, Kent|Globe Lane, Chatham|Images from the Borough of Medway|November 2025 in Chatham, Kent|Chatham Waterfront bus station improvement works (2025)|Road resurfacing in Chatham, Kent

ImageDescription.value:
This night time photograph shows road repair work taking place on Globe Lane during improvements to Chatham Waterfront bus station in Chatham, Kent, England, capturing an active construction site with several vehicles and workers. In the middle of the image is a large white truck with a blue container on the back, owned by Tarmac, a road building company, with an orange flashing light on top displaying the company name TARMAC - A CRH COMPANY on its side. Next to the truck on the right is a yellow JCB digger. The work area is surrounded by blue VolkerHighways barriers to keep people away from the construction zone. Several workers wearing bright orange safety vests are working inside the fenced area, with orange traffic cones, barriers, and bright work lights helping to mark the construction zone and light up the area during the dark evening.

Beginning in September 2025, a programme of upgrades was carried out to improve safety, accessibility and the passenger environment at Chatham Waterfront bus station.[1]

Key changes implemented in 2025 include:

  • Reconfigured traffic flow: The eastern carriageway (Globe Lane/The Paddock) was converted to a one-way northbound lane, and the station’s speed limit was reduced to 10 mph.[2] The road was narrowed and the central traffic island widened, creating a larger pedestrian area. New soft landscaping (shrubs and trees) was planted on the expanded footpath to improve ambience.[3]
  • Upgraded pedestrian crossings: All crossing points and road markings were renewed. In particular, zebra crossings within the station were repainted in a high-visibility light green colour. The crossing in front of the former travel information centre was narrowed.[4]
  • Signage and information: Traffic signs and bus bay signage were refreshed throughout the terminal. New wayfinding signs were installed to guide passengers and drivers safely through the modified layout. (Display screens remained at the outer ends of platforms; some stands were temporarily renumbered while works were in progress.)
  • Surfacing works: The carriageway was resurfaced overnight along the main route from Dock Road through the bus station to the Waterfront Way signal crossing. This required a short full closure of the station during off-peak hours. The resurfacing smooths the roadway and replaces worn areas.
  • Bus stand closures and diversions: During construction the bus stops at Stands A1–A4 (on the eastern side) were closed, and affected routes were diverted to alternative stands within the bus station.[5] Medway Council arranged signage and operator schedules to serve passengers from the remaining open stands. The first phase of works (impacting A1–A4) was completed in mid-November 2025, and those stands reopened on 22 November 2025.

These works were carried out by Medway’s highways contractor (VolkerHighways)[6] and funded by the UK Government's Bus Service Improvement Plan, which the Department for Transport allocated the funding to for the Waterfront bus station. The council emphasised that the scheme’s goal was to enhance pedestrian safety, accessibility (especially for disabled users), and overall public transport integration as part of its wider transport strategy.

The waterfront station was designed by D5 Architects with a focus on openness and integration with the riverside parkland, such as The Paddock and Riverside Gardens. However, the new station faced significant criticism when it opened. A 2012 report noted the “dynamic bus facility” opened in October 2011 five months late and around £2 million over budget.[7] Early post-opening reviews reported many incomplete elements (non-functioning toilets, ticket machines and information screens, missing zebra crossings) and a general sense of a “shambles” among users. Passengers also found the mostly open design unsheltered in bad weather: they complained of being exposed to wind, rain or snow under the limited roof, and even glare from bright sun made LCD displays hard to read. Locals noted that crossing the busy Globe Lane roundabout on foot to reach the station was difficult, and shopkeepers warned that pedestrian access across the road might deter visitors to Chatham town centre. The station’s layout (with stands spread around a large island) was said to create sight-line “blind spots”, making it hard for waiting passengers to spot approaching buses. Overall, while the old Pentagon station (1970s concrete structure) had been criticised as dark and unwelcoming, many people reported a net loss of shelter and convenience with the new waterfront design.

This photo documents part of the £432,000 improvement project that started in September 2025 to make the bus station safer, with work including fixing the road surface, changing traffic flow patterns, and improving safety for people walking, being done at night to avoid disrupting buses and traffic during the day.

Credit.value: Own work, taken with an iPhone 14 Pro.
